_note: The approach, glide, transponder, field, fuel, floor and altitude rules' figures and boundaries, written down from 14 CFR 97.3, 91.119, 91.151, 91.167, 91.175 and 91.177, AC 90-66C, the AIM and NASR's codes, never from the code. Shape and checks as engine/facade/tests/common/cases.rs says; asked by engine/facade/tests/rule_cases.rs.

cases.name: A missed approach down to 787 ft against 700 ft minimums: at or above them
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.175(c): no one may operate below the authorized MDA or continue an approach below the authorized DA/DH unless the runway environment is in sight; the pilot's own minimums are the pilot's.

cases.name: Down to the 700 ft minimums exactly: at them, not under
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.175(c): no one may operate below the authorized MDA or continue an approach below the authorized DA/DH unless the runway environment is in sight; the pilot's own minimums are the pilot's. At the DA or MDA is not below it.

cases.name: A missed approach down to 650 ft against 700 ft minimums: under them, a stop
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.175(c): no one may operate below the authorized MDA or continue an approach below the authorized DA/DH unless the runway environment is in sight; the pilot's own minimums are the pilot's.

cases.name: Below the minimums to land: what 91.175(c) allows with the runway in sight
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.175(c): no one may operate below the authorized MDA or continue an approach below the authorized DA/DH unless the runway environment is in sight; the pilot's own minimums are the pilot's.

cases.name: 5,000 ft, a field 5 nm off at 600 ft, 9 to 1: 5.04 nm of glide, within
cases.source: AC 90-66C (2023) Appendix A: the traffic pattern altitude is usually 1,000 ft above the airport's elevation; a glide is arriving there, so the height to spare is the altitude less the field's elevation and 1,000 ft, flown at the airplane's glide ratio (FAA-H-8083-3C ch. 18, best glide). A nautical mile is 6,076.12 ft.

cases.name: The tanks walked: 40 gal less 1.4 taxi and each leg's burn; filled at the stop; under a 6 gal reserve, low
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and after that, at normal cruise, 30 minutes by day (a)(1), 45 at night (a)(2); 91.167(a)(2) and (3) under IFR: on to the alternate and 45 minutes. 40 - 1.4 - 10 = 28.6; less 20, 8.6; full again, less 1.4 and 34, 4.6.

cases.name: A day flight after a night one is held to its own 30 minutes
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and after that, at normal cruise, 30 minutes by day (a)(1), 45 at night (a)(2); 91.167(a)(2) and (3) under IFR: on to the alternate and 45 minutes. At 10 gph: 45 minutes 7.5 gal, 30 minutes 5; 6.6 is over 5.

cases.name: Under IFR the landing is held to the fuel on to the alternate too
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and after that, at normal cruise, 30 minutes by day (a)(1), 45 at night (a)(2); 91.167(a)(2) and (3) under IFR: on to the alternate and 45 minutes. 6.6 gal is under 5 and 2 more.

cases.name: A leg with no burn known: nothing known after it
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.103: a figure not known is not made up; the tanks after it are not known either.

cases.name: With a stop, the strip's fuel is the first flight's; the second is 3.5 gal short
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and after that, at normal cruise, 30 minutes by day (a)(1), 45 at night (a)(2); 91.167(a)(2) and (3) under IFR: on to the alternate and 45 minutes. Each flight from a fill to a landing needs its own fuel and reserve; the tanks are filled at the stop.

cases.name: Flying the second flight with 10 gal burnt: 19.6 to go
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and after that, at normal cruise, 30 minutes by day (a)(1), 45 at night (a)(2); 91.167(a)(2) and (3) under IFR: on to the alternate and 45 minutes.

cases.name: The highest floor of the pieces, with the lowest ground of all
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.119 (VFR) and 91.177(a)(2) (IFR): the floor holds over all the ground the airplane flies, so along a path of several pieces the highest floor of any of them holds.

cases.name: IFR's floors, no ground
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.119 (VFR) and 91.177(a)(2) (IFR): the floor holds over all the ground the airplane flies, so along a path of several pieces the highest floor of any of them holds.

cases.name: 3,500 ft with a 3,200 ft obstacle: 300 ft, red
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.119(c): "An altitude of 500 feet above the surface ... the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure"; 91.119(b): 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle over a congested area. Red under 500 ft of clearance, yellow under 1,000, exactly 500 meets the rule.

cases.name: 3,500 ft over 3,000 ft of ground: exactly 500, yellow
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.119(c): "An altitude of 500 feet above the surface ... the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure"; 91.119(b): 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle over a congested area. Red under 500 ft of clearance, yellow under 1,000, exactly 500 meets the rule.

cases.name: 3,500 ft over 2,400 ft at most: 1,100, clear
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.119(c): "An altitude of 500 feet above the surface ... the aircraft may not be operated closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure"; 91.119(b): 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle over a congested area. Red under 500 ft of clearance, yellow under 1,000, exactly 500 meets the rule.

cases.name: Crossing 4,500 ft at 40 nm from 6,500: the descent begins 6 nm before
cases.source: The nav log's descent at three to one, three nautical miles for each 1,000 ft (about a 3 degree path, AIM 2-1-2's approach slope; FAA-H-8083-15B ch. 10 plans descents the same way), so 2,000 ft takes 6 nm.

cases.name: Starting down at 40 nm from 6,500 to 4,500: done 6 nm on
cases.source: The nav log's descent at three to one, three nautical miles for each 1,000 ft (about a 3 degree path, AIM 2-1-2's approach slope; FAA-H-8083-15B ch. 10 plans descents the same way), so 2,000 ft takes 6 nm.

cases.name: The wheel's rows: 1,000 to 17,500 ft by 500, highest first
cases.source: The Altitude Advisor's wheel: every 500 ft from 1,000 ft up to 17,500 ft, the last under Class A, which begins at 18,000 ft MSL (14 CFR 71.33, 91.135). Highest first.
